confidence_note: Book not read; Deci study details from Wikipedia and web retellings. Pay per puzzle, break length and exact setup vary by source and are omitted. Old text's 1969 date and controlling-versus-informational feedback lines dropped as unconfirmed. Candle and drawing studies from a summary.
facts: Deci's study was published in 1971 in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology; subjects already showed interest in a puzzle (Soma pieces).
Control group never paid over three days; experimental group unpaid on day 1, paid on day 2, unpaid on day 3.

In a break in the middle of each session subjects could do what they liked (puzzle or magazines such as Time and The New Yorker); the experimenter watched through a one-way window and measured puzzle time.
Paid group spent more break time on the puzzle on day 2 and significantly less on day 3 than the control group.
Pink adds the candle problem (offered money for a fast solution, people did much worse) and a children's drawing study (rewarded children later refused to draw without reward).
Eisenberger and Cameron (1996) argued the day-3 drop may be a reaction to withdrawn reward and that free time is a weak measure.
Pink: pay enough to take money off the table; higher pay improved only basic mechanical tasks.
scene_details: seven puzzle pieces on a table
tension: Paying people for something they already liked seemed to reduce how much they wanted to do it.
opening_idea: The puzzle pieces, the magazines and the experimenter leaving the room.

lessons.idea: Check what a reward turns the task into.
lessons.anchor: day three with the pay gone
